name: Twin Tap
topics_techniques_covered: visual_matching: tap same (smiley) / different (frowny) on two side-by-side patterns as fast as possible
visual_matching: same/not-same when figures differ by one feature (color or an added dot)
visual_matching: identical-or-different judgement on 3/6/9-digit number strings
visual_matching: one-versus-many same/different for older children
one_liner: Two cards flash side by side and the child slams SAME or DIFFERENT as fast as they can while staying correct.
interaction: Two stimuli render simultaneously; the child taps one of two large fixed buttons — a smiley SAME (left) or frowny DIFFERENT (right). The tap submits immediately; the next pair appears after brief feedback. No typing, no scrolling.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows two identical shapes then a hand tapping the smiley (which glows), then two different shapes and the hand tapping the frowny. One unscored warm-up pair with green/red feedback runs before any scored trial.

learning_science.why: Under time pressure children can trade accuracy for speed, so uncontrolled scoring rewards impulsive fast-wrong responding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: RT is credited only on correct trials and the combo breaks on any error, so speed counts only when accuracy is held (M-SPEEDACC).
learning_science.source: Wickelgren, W. A. (1977). Speed-accuracy tradeoff and information processing dynamics. Acta Psychologica, 41(1), 67-85.

learning_science.why: A child's slowest responses correlate with ability more strongly than their fastest, so consistency beats peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Report RT variability (CV) and slow-tail lapse frequency (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) rather than best or mean RT.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A 'worst performance' analysis of individual differences. Intelligence, 14(3), 309-325.

learning_science.why: A novel speeded mechanic must be understood without reading to avoid construct-irrelevant novelty variance.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand demo plus one unscored warm-up trial teach the SAME/DIFFERENT mapping before scoring begins.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59-89.

tail_precision_rationale: Raw same/different speed barely separates the gifted tail, so tail precision comes indirectly: (a) intra-individual consistency - low RT variability and few slow-tail lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) track ability better than peak speed (worst-performance rule); (b) an accuracy-gated speed-accuracy operating point (M-SPEEDACC) that credits speed only when accuracy is held; and (c) engagement gating (M-ENGAGE) that certifies which trials - here and in other sections - reflect real effort. Absolute speed is reported as context, not as a tail decider.
age_rationale: A binary same/different tap needs only a point-and-press motor act, so it spans K-1 (large colored shapes differing by one feature, generous deadline) to 6-8 (3/6/9-digit strings and one-vs-many arrays, short deadline). Stimulus similarity and deadline - not motor demand - set the band, and young bands use oversized buttons to control the Fitts motor confound.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 two large shapes differing by color/shape -> 2-3 pictures differing by one added element -> 4-5 short 3-digit strings -> 6-8 long 6-9 digit strings and one-vs-many arrays
adaptive.difficulty_levers: stimulus similarity, string length, response deadline, mask on/off, proportion of 'same' trials
adaptive.notes: Items are procedurally generated (random strings / shape sets with a controlled number of mismatching features), giving effectively unlimited matched parallel forms for cross-item consistency (M-CONSIST).

engagement_hook: A fast 'twin or not?' arcade round with a smiley/frowny slam, a rising fast-and-correct combo, and a beat-your-streak meter.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Device latency/refresh inflates absolute RT (report device-robust RT variability over raw RT); touch vs mouse differences; visual acuity for fine string differences; a 'press same' response bias (mitigated by balancing trial types); large targets reduce motor (Fitts) noise.

name: Star Sweep
topics_techniques_covered: cancellation: tap every target (e.g., every apple) hidden among other pictures as fast and accurately as possible
cancellation: mobile cancellation that auto-scores hits, false alarms and a concentration-performance index
cancellation: scan rows and mark a conjunction target (a letter d carrying exactly two marks) while ignoring foils
cancellation: structured vs random arrays of picture/letter targets under a time limit
one_liner: A field fills with pictures and the child taps every target as fast as they can while never tapping a non-target.
interaction: A grid/field of target and distractor icons renders; the child taps targets to pop them (they mark as hit). Tapping a distractor logs a false alarm and shatters the combo shield. A block ends on a time budget or when all targets are cleared. Only tapping — no drag, no text.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a hand tapping two targets (which pop) and hovering over a distractor then pulling away (leaving it). One unscored warm-up field with immediate hit/false-alarm feedback precedes scoring.

learning_science.why: Cancellation ability is best captured by combining detections with false-alarm control, not raw sweep speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score CPI = hits - false alarms and gate the combo on correct rejections (M-FALSEALARM, M-COMBO).
learning_science.source: Brickenkamp, R., & Zillmer, E. (1998). The d2 Test of Attention. Hogrefe & Huber.

learning_science.why: Performance drifts as time-on-task grows, so late lapses can bias a speed estimate.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log accuracy/RT drift across the field (M-DRIFT) and discount disengaged late responses.
learning_science.source: Mackworth, N. H. (1948). The breakdown of vigilance during prolonged visual search. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1(1), 6-21.

learning_science.why: Tap time depends on target size and spacing, a motor confound unrelated to processing speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Hold icon size and spacing constant and use large touch targets so speed reflects search, not motor difficulty.
learning_science.source: Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 47(6), 381-391.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Accuracy-gated speed combo
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Rewards sustained joint speed+accuracy rather than impulsive peak speed; a coach-resistant index of controlled processing efficiency that separates children who hold both at pace from those who trade one for the other.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Increment a streak on each response meeting BOTH a correctness check and a per-child adaptive RT band; reset to 0 on any error, false alarm, or timeout; store max streak and the streak distribution.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=30 speeded trials so streak length is estimable.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Commission / false-alarm rate
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Isolates impulsive fast-but-wrong responding so raw speed is never rewarded; separates careful-fast (able) from impulsive-fast responders and underlies the concentration-performance index.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Count taps on non-target/foil stimuli plus anticipatory responses faster than a plausible floor (<150 ms), divided by response opportunities.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=40 target/non-target events with a meaningful foil rate (>=30% non-targets).

tail_precision_rationale: Sweep speed alone is a poor tail signal, so scoring leans on the concentration-performance index (hits minus false alarms), the accuracy-gated combo (M-COMBO), and false-alarm control (M-FALSEALARM): careful-fast children separate from impulsive-fast ones. Drift (M-DRIFT) flags disengagement so any tail decision rests on sustained, engaged performance rather than a lucky fast burst; absolute sweep speed is collateral.
age_rationale: Tapping targets in a field is motor-simple and works from K-1 (tap apples among two fruit types, large icons) to 6-8 (conjunction targets among confusable foils). Field density and foil similarity - not motor demand - set the band; young bands use fewer, larger icons and a picture (non-reading) target.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 tap apples among two fruit types -> 2-3 tap one picture target among 3-4 foils -> 4-5 letter/shape target among similar foils -> 6-8 conjunction target (d with exactly two marks) among confusable foils
adaptive.difficulty_levers: field density, target:distractor ratio, foil similarity, single-feature vs conjunction target, time budget
adaptive.notes: Fields are generated from a target/foil grammar with known hit/false-alarm keys, so CPI and combo score automatically and unlimited matched fields can be cloned.

engagement_hook: A satisfying 'pop every star' sweep with a combo that only grows on clean taps and a shield that shatters on a wrong tap.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Screen size limits field density; motor speed and tap accuracy (mitigated by large icons and constant spacing); prior game familiarity (mitigated by ghost-hand + warm-up); reading is avoided by using picture targets at young bands.

name: Secret Decoder
topics_techniques_covered: coding_digit_symbol: on-screen DSST where a 1-9 symbol key sits on screen and the child taps the symbol matching each presented digit
coding_digit_symbol: match each picture to its partner shape using a small two-row key, as many pairs as possible before time runs out
coding_digit_symbol: copy the symbol corresponding to each geometric shape or number using a printed key
coding_digit_symbol: scrolling digit-symbol substitution scoring correct matches and average time per correct match
one_liner: Using a visible key, the child taps the symbol that matches each incoming digit/shape, decoding as many as possible before the timer runs out.
interaction: A fixed key (digit/shape -> symbol pairs) sits at the top. A single prompt digit/shape appears in a slot; the child taps the matching symbol from a response row beneath. A correct tap advances to the next prompt; a wrong tap flashes red and stays until corrected. Tapping only; key stays visible.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the prompt digit, the hand tracing up to that digit in the key, then tapping the matching symbol below (which locks in). One unscored warm-up match with the key highlighted precedes the timed block.

learning_science.principle: Digit-Symbol / Coding as a processing-speed marker
learning_science.why: Symbol substitution under time is a long-validated index of clerical/processing speed in child batteries.
learning_science.concrete_decision: On-screen coding with a fixed visible key; score correct matches per unit time plus per-match consistency.
learning_science.source: Wechsler, D. (2014). WISC-V Technical and Interpretive Manual (Coding / Processing Speed Index). Pearson.

learning_science.why: Consistency of substitution speed tracks ability better than the single fastest match.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Emphasize RT variability and slow-tail lapses across matches (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE), not peak match speed.
learning_science.source: Coyle, T. R. (2003). A review of the worst performance rule. Intelligence, 31(6), 567-587.

learning_science.why: Looking between a distant key and the item adds load, so a novel child may fail for layout reasons rather than speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep the key and item on one screen and teach via a ghost-hand look-up plus one warm-up match.
learning_science.source: Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (1992). The split-attention effect as a factor in the design of instruction. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 62(2), 233-246.

tail_precision_rationale: Coding throughput has low standalone tail discrimination and is coachable, so the sharper signals are substitution consistency (M-RTVAR) and slow-tail lapses (M-LAPSE) on correct matches, plus the speed-accuracy point (M-SPEEDACC). Randomizing the key each session blunts practice inflation. Its tail value is mainly as corroborating efficiency and engagement evidence, not a primary separator.
age_rationale: Coding requires holding a key and cross-referencing, so it starts at 2-3 (3-4 picture-symbol pairs, mirroring WISC Coding Form A used at ages 6-7) and extends to 6-8 (full 1-9 digit-symbol). It is excluded from K-1 because key cross-referencing - not motor speed - would dominate and unfairly penalize kindergarteners.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 three-to-four picture-symbol pairs -> 4-5 six digit-symbol pairs -> 6-8 full 1-9 digit-symbol key
adaptive.difficulty_levers: key size (number of pairs), symbol confusability, key always-visible vs briefly hidden (adds working memory), time budget
adaptive.notes: Key mappings are randomized per session (anti-practice); correct/incorrect is deterministic from the key, so parallel forms are unlimited.

engagement_hook: A spy 'crack the code' race against a shrinking timer with a live decode counter and a combo chain for clean fast matches.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Split-attention/layout load if key and item are far apart (kept adjacent); symbol confusability and fine motor for small targets (large targets used); practice/familiarity with coding (key randomized per session); no reading beyond digit/shape recognition is required.

name: Target Hunt
topics_techniques_covered: symbol_search: arcade tap-the-target with a visible accuracy meter; the combo builds only on correct AND fast taps and breaks on any false alarm
symbol_search: look at a target shape, then tap it when it appears among distractors sliding across, ignoring non-matches
symbol_search: scan a search group and mark whether either of two target symbols is present, row by row against the clock
symbol_search: visual search where RT and accuracy scale with set size and target-distractor similarity
one_liner: A target symbol is shown, then shapes stream across a lane and the child taps only the ones that match, as fast as possible without hitting foils.
interaction: One or two target symbols pin to the left. Symbols then slide across a lane; the child taps matches before they exit (a hit pops them) and must not tap foils (a false alarm). A visible accuracy meter and combo update live. Tapping only; a block runs on a timer.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the pinned target, a matching symbol sliding in and the hand tapping it (pop), then a foil sliding by while the hand deliberately does not tap. One unscored warm-up lane with feedback precedes scoring.

learning_science.why: RT rises with the number and similarity of distractors, giving a graded, calibratable difficulty lever.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale set size and target-distractor similarity to titrate difficulty and log RT against set size.
learning_science.source: Treisman, A., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

learning_science.why: An arcade tap task invites impulsive taps, so false alarms must cost more than a hit rewards.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The combo builds only on correct+fast taps and breaks on any false alarm (M-COMBO, M-FALSEALARM, M-SPEEDACC).
learning_science.source: Wickelgren, W. A. (1977). Speed-accuracy tradeoff and information processing dynamics. Acta Psychologica, 41(1), 67-85.

learning_science.why: The tap-only-matches rule must be obvious without any text.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand taps a matching symbol and visibly ignores a foil before scoring starts.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59-89.

tail_precision_rationale: Search speed is weakly diagnostic on its own, so the tail contribution is the joint speed-accuracy operating point under an accuracy gate (M-SPEEDACC, M-COMBO) and false-alarm suppression (M-FALSEALARM), which distinguish controlled fast search from impulsive tapping. The set-size RT pattern adds a rate signal, but absolute speed is treated as collateral rather than decisive.
age_rationale: Scanning for a held target among distractors needs stable comparison, appropriate from 2-3 (distinct shapes, small set size, slow slide) to 6-8 (two similar target symbols, larger sets, fast slide). K-1 is excluded because abstract-symbol search confounds speed with an emerging comparison skill; K-1 speed is captured instead by the matching, sweep, whack, and naming types.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 tap a distinct shape among 2 foils -> 4-5 more foils at moderate similarity -> 6-8 two target symbols among many confusable foils (WISC Symbol Search-like)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: set size, target-distractor similarity, slide speed, number of simultaneous targets, foil rate
adaptive.notes: Symbols are drawn from a large glyph pool with a tunable similarity metric, giving unlimited matched forms.

engagement_hook: An arcade lane where targets slide by and you snipe only the matches; the accuracy meter and combo reward clean, fast hits and punish trigger-happy taps.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Impulsivity inflating false alarms (penalized via combo break); slide speed interacts with device frame rate; target-distractor similarity must be perceptually calibrated; large targets limit the motor confound.

name: Whack-It
topics_techniques_covered: simple_reaction_time: arcade whack-it - tap the critter the moment it pops up; the combo rewards fast AND correct hits while tapping an empty hole breaks it
simple_reaction_time: press the instant a single stimulus appears over many trials; record mean and (critically) RT variability
choice_reaction_time: tap the left or right target depending on which side a friendly animal appears (two-choice)
choice_reaction_time: choice reaction across 1/2/4 alternatives; the slope of RT against log2(choices) indexes processing rate (Hick's law)
choice_reaction_time: derive intra-individual RT variability and lapse frequency per the worst-performance rule
one_liner: Critters pop out of holes and the child taps them the instant they appear (or taps the correct hole), with peeking-too-early penalized.
interaction: One or more holes are shown. After a jittered delay a critter pops from a hole; the child taps it (simple RT) or taps the hole it appeared in (choice RT). A tap before the pop is a false start; too slow is a miss. Feedback flashes, then the next trial. Tapping only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a critter popping and the hand tapping it fast (combo ticks up), then the hand tapping too early and the combo breaking. One unscored warm-up pop precedes the scored block.

learning_science.why: Choice RT increases linearly with log2(number of alternatives), and that slope indexes information-processing rate.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer 1/2/4 holes as difficulty levers and derive the RT-vs-log2(N) slope (M-HICKSLOPE), separating central rate from a motor/device intercept.
learning_science.source: Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 4(1), 11-26.

learning_science.why: Intra-individual RT variability and lapses predict ability better than mean or fastest RT.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Emphasize RT CV and slow-tail lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE); never score peak speed.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A 'worst performance' analysis of individual differences. Intelligence, 14(3), 309-325.

learning_science.why: Very fast 'responses' before the stimulus are guesses, not perception.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Flag responses under 150 ms as false starts (anticipations) that break the combo and are excluded from RT (M-FALSEALARM).
learning_science.source: Luce, R. D. (1986). Response Times: Their Role in Inferring Elementary Mental Organization. Oxford University Press.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Hick's-law RT slope
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: A device- and base-motor-robust estimate of information-processing RATE: the intercept absorbs motor/device latency while the slope reflects central processing, so it is less confounded than absolute RT at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Administer blocks at 1, 2, and 4 response alternatives; regress mean correct RT on log2(N) and store slope and intercept.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=15 correct trials per set size (>=45 total) for a stable slope.

tail_precision_rationale: Peak reaction time is famously weak and confounded, so this type deliberately scores the parts of the RT distribution that DO track ability: intra-individual variability and slow-tail lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE; worst-performance rule) and the Hick slope (M-HICKSLOPE), whose intercept absorbs motor/device latency so the slope is a cleaner central-rate estimate. Anticipations are flagged (M-FALSEALARM). Even so its standalone tail power is modest and is framed as one converging signal.
age_rationale: Detecting and tapping a pop-up is the most motor-basic speeded act, so simple RT fits K-1 (one hole, huge target). Choice RT (two then four holes) is layered for 2-3 through 6-8 to derive the Hick slope. Target size is held constant across bands to control the motor (Fitts) confound.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 one hole (simple RT) -> 2-3 two holes (2-choice) -> 4-5 four holes -> 6-8 four holes with a short deadline and catch (no-pop) trials
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of holes (Hick N), inter-stimulus interval jitter, response deadline, proportion of catch trials
adaptive.notes: Trials are fully parametric (N, ISI, deadline); the RT-vs-log2(N) slope is computed across blocks and stimuli are trivially cloneable.

engagement_hook: Whack-the-critter the instant it pops - too eager (a false start) breaks your combo, so cool, precise timing wins the streak.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Anticipatory false starts (flagged <150 ms); device input latency (report variability and the Hick slope, whose intercept absorbs device/motor latency); touch vs mouse differences; fatigue on long blocks (drift logged).

name: Blink Towers
topics_techniques_covered: inspection_time: two lines/towers of different length flash briefly then are masked; report which side was longer (motor-free perceptual intake)
inspection_time: two towers flash then vanish behind a mask; the child taps the taller tower afterward at their leisure; accuracy at very short exposures is the index
inspection_time: backward-masked brief discrimination presented as a motor-free index of perceptual intake speed
one_liner: Two towers flash for a split second and are then hidden by a mask; the child calmly taps which one was taller, with the flash getting shorter each round.
interaction: Two towers appear for a staircased exposure, then a pattern mask overwrites them. Only after the mask does the child tap the taller side (a large LEFT / RIGHT choice). The response itself is untimed (motor-free); the manipulated variable is the pre-mask exposure. Tapping only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the towers flash, the mask drop, and the hand calmly tapping the side that was taller (checkmark), emphasizing that answering is unhurried. One unscored warm-up with a long exposure precedes the staircase.

learning_science.why: The exposure needed to discriminate a masked stimulus correlates (modestly) with g and is largely motor-free.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Backward-masked two-tower discrimination with an untimed response; estimate the exposure threshold (M-ITTHRESH).
learning_science.source: Deary, I. J., & Stough, C. (1996). Intelligence and inspection time. American Psychologist, 51(6), 599-608.

learning_science.why: Sets honest expectations: inspection time is a real but modest correlate, best used as one signal among many.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Report the IT threshold as a motor-robust adjunct, never as a standalone tail decider.
learning_science.source: Grudnik, J. L., & Kranzler, J. H. (2001). Meta-analysis of the relationship between intelligence and inspection time. Intelligence, 29(6), 523-535.

learning_science.why: The mask removes the stimulus so motor/response speed cannot inflate the score.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present a pattern mask after a staircased exposure and let the child answer at leisure (motor-free).
learning_science.source: Vickers, D., Nettelbeck, T., & Willson, R. J. (1972). Perceptual indices of performance: A theory and its application to the study of intelligence. Perception, 1(3), 263-295.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Inspection-time threshold
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: A near motor-free, practice-resistant index of perceptual intake speed - the processing-speed measure with the cleanest (still modest) link to g and the least motor/device confound, making it the most defensible single speed adjunct at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Staircase the pre-mask exposure duration (e.g., 2-down/1-up) in a backward-masked two-alternative discrimination and estimate the exposure at the target accuracy (~71-75% correct).
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=40-60 masked trials for a stable staircase threshold; report threshold in ms alongside the measured display frame time.

tail_precision_rationale: Inspection time is the least motor- and practice-confounded speed measure and has the cleanest (still modest, r approx -0.3 to -0.5) link to g, so its threshold (M-ITTHRESH) is the most defensible single processing-speed tail adjunct - useful precisely because the response is untimed and motor-free. It is offered as a corroborating perceptual-intake index, never as a standalone tail decider.
age_rationale: The masked-discrimination response is untimed and motor-free, so difficulty is perceptual, not motor. It fits 2-3 (large height difference, long ~300-400 ms exposures) to 6-8 (small differences, short staircased exposures). At 2-3 exposures stay long and data are noisier, so it serves mainly as engagement plus a coarse perceptual screen; K-1 is excluded because understanding the flash-then-mask rule is unreliable that young.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 large height difference, ~300-400 ms exposure -> 4-5 moderate difference, ~150-250 ms -> 6-8 small difference, staircased down toward ~30-80 ms
adaptive.difficulty_levers: pre-mask exposure duration (staircase), height-difference magnitude, mask strength, inter-trial interval
adaptive.notes: A 2-down/1-up staircase converges on the ~71% threshold; the two bars are generated, so items are infinitely cloneable and the threshold is a single robust statistic.

engagement_hook: A blink-and-you-miss-it towers duel: the flash gets shorter every round and you still have to call the taller tower - how short can you go?
construct_irrelevant_risks: Display refresh rate limits the shortest true exposure (report the threshold with the measured frame time); ambient brightness and visual acuity; sustained-attention lapses; but it is the least motor-confounded speed task because the response is untimed.

name: Speed Namer
topics_techniques_covered: rapid_automatized_naming: name a grid of repeated color patches (red, blue, green, black) as fast as possible - a pre-literacy naming-speed measure
rapid_automatized_naming: name a grid of repeated familiar objects (ball, dog, star) left-to-right as fast as possible; score is total time and errors
rapid_automatized_naming: rapid letter/digit naming as fast as possible; alphanumeric RAN most linked to reading fluency
rapid_automatized_naming: contrast serial (full-grid) naming, which requires sustained scanning and eye-movements, against discrete naming
one_liner: The child moves left-to-right across a grid of repeated items, tapping each as they name it aloud, keeping a smooth, fast rhythm.
interaction: A serial grid of repeated items renders. The child names each item aloud and taps it to advance (tap-to-advance), moving strictly left-to-right, top-to-bottom; the current item is highlighted. Each tap timestamps the inter-item interval. Total time, rhythm, and hesitations are logged. (Optional on-device speech can supplement, but tapping is the scored channel.)
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a hand tapping across the first row in a steady beat with a little 'speech' puff over each item, then continuing to the next row. One unscored warm-up row precedes the scored grid.

learning_science.why: Serial naming speed of familiar items is a robust correlate of reading fluency and processing speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a serial grid of repeated colors/objects/letters/digits and score total time plus inter-item rhythm.
learning_science.source: Norton, E. S., & Wolf, M. (2012). Rapid automatized naming (RAN) and reading fluency: Implications for understanding and treatment of reading disabilities. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 427-452.

learning_science.why: Serial (full-grid) naming captures the scanning and eye-movement demands that discrete single-item naming misses.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a full-grid serial layout with tap-to-advance to capture the serial rhythm and hesitations.
learning_science.source: Denckla, M. B., & Rudel, R. G. (1976). Rapid automatized naming (R.A.N.): Dyslexia differentiated from other learning disabilities. Neuropsychologia, 14(4), 471-479.

learning_science.why: Inter-item pauses, not peak articulation speed, carry much of the naming-ability signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log inter-item-interval variability and long hesitations as lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) rather than crediting the single fastest item.
learning_science.source: Kail, R., & Hall, L. K. (1994). Processing speed, naming speed, and reading. Developmental Psychology, 30(6), 949-954.

tail_precision_rationale: Naming speed predicts fluency more than g, so its tail value is narrow: rhythm consistency (M-RTVAR) and hesitation/lapse frequency (M-LAPSE) across the serial grid, plus drift (M-DRIFT), index automaticity and sustained engagement. It is best read as collateral fluency/effort evidence and a screen for disfluency, not as a gifted-tail separator.
age_rationale: Tap-to-advance serial naming needs only sequential taps, so it spans K-1 (5 colors or objects - pre-literacy naming) to 6-8 (letters/digits, denser grids). Content, not motor demand, sets the band: pre-readers name colors/objects while readers name letters/digits.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 grid of 5 repeated colors or objects -> 2-3 letters/digits in a 5x5 grid -> 4-5 denser mixed alphanumeric -> 6-8 dense letter/digit grids
adaptive.difficulty_levers: item type (color/object vs letter/digit), grid density, item confusability, row length
adaptive.notes: Grids are generated from an item pool; tap-to-advance yields rhythm and hesitation metrics without requiring voice capture, though optional on-device speech can corroborate.

engagement_hook: A rhythm run: name and tap across the grid to keep a smooth beat - hesitations break the groove and your rhythm meter shows it live.
construct_irrelevant_risks: True RAN requires voice capture; tap-to-advance is a serial-scanning proxy that could be gamed by tapping without naming (mitigated by rhythm-consistency checks and optional on-device speech); item familiarity/reading level (colors/objects for pre-readers); a motor tapping-speed floor.

name: Twin Finder
topics_techniques_covered: visual_matching: in each row of six items find and mark the two that are identical, completing as many rows as possible within a time limit (early rows use small/simple items)
visual_matching: locate the two identical letter/number clusters in a row of six, working as fast as possible (orthographic perceptual speed)
visual_matching: same/not-same among items differing by one feature (a color or an added element) applied within a row
cancellation: locate a specific repeated pair of pictures as quickly as possible, ignoring all other pictures
one_liner: A row of six items appears and the child taps the two that are exactly identical, then the next row loads, clearing as many rows as possible before time runs out.
interaction: Each row shows six items; exactly two are identical and the other four each differ by one feature. The child taps the first twin then its match; a correct pair pops and the next row slides in. Tapping a non-matching item logs a miss and shakes the row. Tapping only, no drag, no text.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a hand scanning the row left-to-right, hovering over items, then tapping the two that match (which pop together). One unscored warm-up row with green/red feedback precedes scoring.

learning_science.why: Rapidly locating identical items in a row is a long-validated perceptual-speed marker in child cognitive batteries.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a six-item row with exactly one identical pair and score rows cleared plus per-row time; the response is finding a pair, not a binary same/different judgement.
learning_science.source: Woodcock, R. W., McGrew, K. S., & Mather, N. (2001). Woodcock-Johnson III Tests of Cognitive Abilities (Visual Matching). Riverside.

learning_science.why: Per-row time consistency tracks ability better than the single fastest row.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Report per-row time variability and slow-row drift (M-RTVAR, M-DRIFT) rather than best row time.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A worst performance analysis of individual differences. Intelligence, 14(3), 309-325.

learning_science.why: Finding the matching pair requires scanning and comparing, so scan efficiency is part of the signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log the tap sequence and first-action latency (M-PATH, M-RTFIRST) to index scan strategy, not just the outcome.
learning_science.source: Treisman, A., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

tail_precision_rationale: Within-row find-identical speed is weakly diagnostic on its own, so tail precision comes from per-row time consistency (M-RTVAR) and slow-row drift (M-DRIFT; worst-performance rule), reflective first-scan latency (M-RTFIRST), and scan-path efficiency (M-PATH). Absolute rows-per-minute is reported as context, not a tail decider, and engagement (M-ENGAGE) certifies effort.
age_rationale: Tapping the two matching items in a row is motor-simple, so it spans K-1 (a short row of 4 large pictures with one obvious pair) to 6-8 (rows of six 3-9 digit or letter clusters differing by one feature). Row length and feature subtlety, not motor demand, set the band; young bands use large picture items to control the Fitts motor confound and avoid reading.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 row of 4 large pictures with one identical pair -> 2-3 row of 5 simple shapes differing by one feature -> 4-5 six short digit strings -> 6-8 six 6-9 digit or letter clusters differing by one feature
adaptive.difficulty_levers: row length, feature-difference subtlety, string length, foil similarity, time budget
adaptive.notes: Rows are procedurally generated from an item grammar with exactly one keyed identical pair, giving unlimited matched parallel forms and automatic scoring.

engagement_hook: A speed hunt for the matching twins hiding in each row - pop the pair and the next row rushes in while a rows-cleared meter climbs.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Visual acuity for fine one-feature differences; row length interacts with motor scan time (large items, constant spacing); reading is avoided with picture items at young bands; device/touch differences (report per-row consistency over raw speed).

name: Match Chute
topics_techniques_covered: visual_matching: same/not-same judgement on two visual patterns that may differ by color, by adding or removing an element, or (for older children) one-versus-many
visual_matching: decide if two simple figures are the same or different when they differ by one feature (a color or an added dot)
visual_matching: side-by-side same/different judgement streamed continuously as a flowing conveyor of cards against a fixed reference
visual_matching: decide whether two number strings (3, 6, or 9 digits) are identical or different
one_liner: A reference card is pinned at the top while single cards flow down a chute; the child sends each card LEFT if it matches the reference or RIGHT if it differs, fast but correct.
interaction: A persistent reference pattern sits at the top. Candidate cards descend one at a time; the child taps a large MATCH (left) or DIFFERENT (right) chute to route each card before it reaches the floor. A correct route banks the card and grows a combo; a wrong route or a card that hits the floor breaks the combo. Routing taps only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a card that matches the reference being pushed left into a green chute, then a differing card pushed right into an orange chute. One unscored warm-up card with feedback precedes scoring.

learning_science.why: A flowing conveyor invites impulsive routing, so speed must be credited only when accuracy is held.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The combo builds only on correct routes and breaks on any wrong route or miss (M-COMBO, M-SPEEDACC).
learning_science.source: Wickelgren, W. A. (1977). Speed-accuracy tradeoff and information processing dynamics. Acta Psychologica, 41(1), 67-85.

learning_science.why: Same/different routing conflates sensitivity with a left/right response bias, which must be separated.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Compute d-prime from hits and false alarms so a cautious router and a guesser are not scored alike (M-DPRIME).
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

learning_science.why: The match-left / differ-right mapping must be obvious without any text.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand routes a matching card left and a differing card right before scoring begins.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59-89.

tail_precision_rationale: Routing speed alone barely separates the tail, so scoring leans on signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) that removes left/right response bias, the accuracy-gated combo (M-COMBO) and speed-accuracy operating point (M-SPEEDACC) that credit speed only when accuracy is held, and drift (M-DRIFT) that gates engagement. Absolute throughput is collateral, never a standalone tail decider.
age_rationale: Routing a card left or right is a point-and-press act, so it spans K-1 (two large shapes differing by color, slow descent, generous floor) to 6-8 (6-9 digit strings and one-versus-many arrays, fast descent). Reference-candidate similarity and descent speed, not motor demand, set the band; oversized chutes control the Fitts motor confound at young bands.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 two large shapes differing by color -> 2-3 figures differing by one added element -> 4-5 short 3-digit strings -> 6-8 6-9 digit strings and one-versus-many arrays
adaptive.difficulty_levers: reference-candidate similarity, descent speed, string length, one-versus-many, proportion of matches, floor deadline
adaptive.notes: Reference and candidates are procedurally generated with a controlled number of mismatching features and a balanced match rate, giving unlimited matched forms and automatic hit/false-alarm keys.

engagement_hook: A conveyor-sorting arcade - flick each card into the right chute before it drops, and a clean-routing combo climbs while a wrong flick shatters it.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Descent speed interacts with device frame rate (report d-prime and consistency over raw throughput); a left/right or match-side response bias (mitigated by balancing trial types and reporting d-prime); visual acuity for fine differences; large chutes limit the motor confound.

name: Code Check
topics_techniques_covered: coding_digit_symbol: using a fixed visible key that pairs each digit 1-9 with a symbol, judge whether a presented digit-symbol pairing matches the key
coding_digit_symbol: match each picture to its partner shape using a small two-row key (verify presented picture-shape pairings)
coding_digit_symbol: on-screen digit-symbol substitution against a fixed visible key, scored on correct decisions per unit time
coding_digit_symbol: copy or verify the symbol corresponding to each geometric shape or number using a printed key
one_liner: A digit-symbol key sits on screen while pairs flash by; the child taps a check if the pair matches the key or a cross if it is a broken code, as fast as possible.
interaction: A fixed key (each digit paired to a symbol) is shown. A single digit-symbol pair appears in a slot; the child taps a large green CHECK (matches the key) or red CROSS (does not match). A correct decision advances to the next pair; an error flashes red. Tapping only; the key stays visible throughout.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the hand tracing from the pair's digit up to that digit in the key, seeing the symbol match, and tapping the check; then a mismatched pair and the hand tapping the cross. One unscored warm-up decision precedes the timed block.

learning_science.principle: Digit-Symbol / Coding as a processing-speed marker
learning_science.why: Symbol-digit cross-referencing under time is a long-validated index of clerical/processing speed in child batteries.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep a fixed visible key and score correct match/mismatch decisions per unit time plus decision consistency.
learning_science.source: Wechsler, D. (2014). WISC-V Technical and Interpretive Manual (Coding / Processing Speed Index). Pearson.

learning_science.why: Verifying pairings is detecting mismatches, so sensitivity must be separated from a yes/no response bias.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Compute d-prime and the false-alarm rate so a careful checker and a guesser are not scored alike (M-DPRIME, M-FALSEALARM).
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

learning_science.why: Looking between a distant key and the pair adds load unrelated to speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep the key and the pair on one screen and teach the look-up via a ghost-hand plus one warm-up decision.
learning_science.source: Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (1992). The split-attention effect as a factor in the design of instruction. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 62(2), 233-246.

tail_precision_rationale: Verification throughput is coachable and weak alone, so the sharper signals are signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) and false-alarm control (M-FALSEALARM), which distinguish true mismatch detection from guessing, plus the accuracy-gated speed-accuracy point (M-SPEEDACC). Randomizing the key each session blunts practice inflation; drift (M-DRIFT) gates engagement. Its tail value is corroborating efficiency evidence, not a primary separator.
age_rationale: Verifying a pairing requires holding a key and cross-referencing, so it starts at 2-3 (3-4 picture-symbol pairs) and extends to 6-8 (full 1-9 digit-symbol). K-1 is excluded because key cross-referencing, not perceptual speed, would dominate and unfairly penalize kindergarteners; their coding speed is captured by tap-select and matching types.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 three-to-four picture-symbol pairs -> 4-5 six digit-symbol pairs -> 6-8 full 1-9 digit-symbol key
adaptive.difficulty_levers: key size (number of pairs), symbol confusability, proportion of broken pairs, key always-visible vs briefly hidden, time budget
adaptive.notes: Key mappings are randomized per session (anti-practice) and match/mismatch is deterministic from the key with a balanced broken rate, so parallel forms and hit/false-alarm keys are unlimited.

engagement_hook: A code-inspector race - bust the broken codes as they flash by, with a clean-call combo that only grows on fast correct decisions.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Split-attention/layout load if key and pair are far apart (kept adjacent); symbol confusability and fine targets (large targets used); a yes/no response bias (balanced broken rate and d-prime reporting); practice with a fixed key (randomized per session); no reading beyond digit/shape recognition.

name: Glyph Writer
topics_techniques_covered: coding_digit_symbol: using a key that pairs each digit 1-9 with a symbol, write (trace) the symbol that matches each digit as fast as possible
coding_digit_symbol: copy the symbol that corresponds to each geometric shape or number using a printed key, working as fast as possible within the time limit
coding_digit_symbol: scrolling digit-symbol substitution that scores correct matches and average time per correct match
one_liner: Using a visible key, the child traces the symbol that matches each incoming digit inside a large box, decoding as many as possible before the timer runs out.
interaction: A fixed key (each digit paired to a symbol) is shown. A prompt digit appears; the child traces the matching symbol over a faint template in a large writing box with finger, stylus, or mouse. Releasing submits the stroke and a shape-matcher checks whether the traced glyph matches the keyed symbol (neatness is not scored). A correct glyph advances; a mismatch clears the box to retry. Tracing only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the hand looking up the prompt digit in the key, then tracing the matching glyph in the box as a dotted path fills in. One unscored warm-up trace with the key highlighted precedes the timed block.

learning_science.principle: Digit-Symbol / Coding production as a processing-speed marker
learning_science.why: The classic Coding subtest has children write the symbol for each digit, making written substitution a validated speed marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Reproduce the write-the-symbol response digitally via guided tracing and score correct glyphs per unit time.
learning_science.source: Wechsler, D. (2014). WISC-V Technical and Interpretive Manual (Coding / Processing Speed Index). Pearson.

learning_science.why: Consistency of substitution speed tracks ability better than the single fastest glyph.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Emphasize inter-glyph time variability (M-RTVAR) on correct glyphs rather than peak production speed.
learning_science.source: Coyle, T. R. (2003). A review of the worst performance rule. Intelligence, 31(6), 567-587.

learning_science.why: Tracing adds a graphomotor component that can confound a pure speed estimate.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a large template-guided box, score glyph identity not neatness, and report consistency and stroke path (M-PATH, M-REV) rather than raw production speed.
learning_science.source: Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 47(6), 381-391.

tail_precision_rationale: Production throughput is motor-confounded and coachable, so tail value rests on substitution consistency (M-RTVAR) and clean stroke paths (M-PATH) with few re-traces (M-REV) on correct glyphs, with drift (M-DRIFT) gating engagement. It is framed as collateral efficiency/engagement evidence and explicitly not a standalone tail separator, because motor production adds construct-irrelevant variance.
age_rationale: Tracing a glyph adds a fine-motor production demand absent from tap-select coding, so it starts at 4-5 where graphomotor control is adequate and large template-guided boxes bound the motor confound; 6-8 uses the full key with fainter guidance. K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because graphomotor variance would swamp the speed signal at those ages, which are covered by tap-select coding instead.

adaptive.content_range: 4-5 six digit-symbol pairs with a strong tracing template -> 6-8 full 1-9 key with a faint or no template and more confusable glyphs
adaptive.difficulty_levers: key size, template guidance strength, glyph stroke complexity, box size, time budget
adaptive.notes: Key mappings are randomized per session (anti-practice); glyph identity is checked by a template shape-matcher so scoring is deterministic and parallel forms are unlimited.

engagement_hook: A secret-code writer - draw each glyph faster and faster as a decode counter climbs, with a combo for clean quick traces.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor/graphomotor variance (mitigated by a large box, a template guide, scoring glyph identity not neatness, and reporting consistency over raw speed); stylus vs finger vs mouse differences; split-attention if key and box are far apart (kept adjacent); practice with a fixed key (randomized per session).

name: Line Sweeper
topics_techniques_covered: cancellation: tap all targets in each row before it advances; auto-score hits, false alarms and a concentration-performance index (mobile row-by-row cancellation)
cancellation: cross out or tap every target letter (for example every letter d) hidden in rows of similar letters, as fast and accurately as possible
cancellation: scan timed rows and mark every d carrying exactly two marks while ignoring d's with other numbers of marks and all p's (conjunction target)
cancellation: scan a structured array of pictures and mark the target objects within a time limit
one_liner: One row of items is active at a time; the child taps every target in that row, then it advances, sweeping down structured rows against the clock without tapping foils.
interaction: Rows are stacked vertically and only the current row is highlighted and tappable. The child taps each target in the active row (targets mark as hit) while a tap on a foil logs a false alarm. Clearing all targets, or tapping a NEXT arrow, advances to the next row, enforcing left-to-right, row-by-row scanning. Tapping only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop sweeps the active row left-to-right, taps the two targets (which mark), skips a foil, then taps NEXT to advance. One unscored warm-up row with hit/false-alarm feedback precedes scoring.

learning_science.why: Cancellation ability is best captured by combining detections with false-alarm control across structured rows, not raw sweep speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score a concentration-performance index (hits minus false alarms) row by row and enforce serial scanning by activating one row at a time.
learning_science.source: Brickenkamp, R., & Zillmer, E. (1998). The d2 Test of Attention. Hogrefe & Huber.

learning_science.why: Accuracy and speed drift as time-on-task grows, so late-row lapses can bias an estimate.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log accuracy/time drift across rows (M-DRIFT) and discount disengaged late rows.
learning_science.source: Mackworth, N. H. (1948). The breakdown of vigilance during prolonged visual search. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1(1), 6-21.

learning_science.why: Row cancellation mixes true target detection with false alarms, which must be separated from response bias.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Compute d-prime from row hits and false alarms so cautious and impulsive sweepers are not scored alike (M-DPRIME, M-FALSEALARM).
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: Rows-per-minute alone is a poor tail signal, so scoring leans on the concentration-performance index via signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) and false-alarm control (M-FALSEALARM), per-row time consistency (M-RTVAR), and drift across rows (M-DRIFT) that certifies sustained, engaged performance. The row-scan path (M-PATH) indexes scanning discipline; absolute sweep speed is collateral.
age_rationale: Tapping targets in a highlighted row is motor-simple, working from K-1 (short rows, a picture target, large icons) to 6-8 (conjunction targets among confusable foils in dense rows). Row length and foil similarity, not motor demand, set the band; young bands use fewer, larger icons and a non-reading picture target.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 short rows, tap the apples among two fruit types -> 2-3 one picture target among 3-4 foils -> 4-5 a letter/shape target among similar foils -> 6-8 a conjunction target (d with exactly two marks) among confusable foils in dense rows
adaptive.difficulty_levers: row length, target:foil ratio, foil similarity, single-feature vs conjunction target, number of rows, time budget
adaptive.notes: Rows are generated from a target/foil grammar with known hit/false-alarm keys, so the concentration-performance index scores automatically and unlimited matched rows can be cloned.

engagement_hook: Sweep each glowing line clean before the next lights up - a line-clear streak and a rows-per-minute meter reward disciplined left-to-right scanning.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor scan speed and tap accuracy (mitigated by large icons and constant spacing); reading is avoided with picture targets at young bands; screen size limits row length; false alarms are penalized via the concentration-performance index; drift is logged to discount disengaged rows.

name: Rhythm Switch
topics_techniques_covered: rapid_automatized_naming: contrast serial (full-grid) rapid naming with an alternating (rapid alternating stimulus) grid that switches category each item, capturing scanning plus set-switching
rapid_automatized_naming: name a grid of repeated colors or familiar objects as fast as possible (single-category baseline)
rapid_automatized_naming: name a grid of repeated letters or digits as fast as possible (alphanumeric naming most linked to reading fluency)
one_liner: The child taps across a grid naming each item aloud, but the grid alternates categories (a color, then a shape, then a color) so they must switch naming sets in rhythm.
interaction: A serial grid whose items alternate between two categories (for example a color patch and an object, or a letter and a digit). The child names each item aloud and taps it to advance, moving strictly left-to-right, top-to-bottom; the current item is highlighted and each tap timestamps the inter-item interval. A single-category baseline block and the alternating block are compared. Tapping is the scored channel; optional on-device speech can corroborate.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop taps across the first row in a steady beat with a little speech puff over each item, visibly switching between a color and a shape each step. One unscored warm-up row precedes the scored grid.

learning_science.why: Alternating-category naming predicts reading fluency beyond single-category RAN by adding a switching demand.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an alternating grid and contrast it with a single-category baseline to isolate the switching component.
learning_science.source: Wolf, M. (1986). Rapid alternating stimulus naming in the developmental dyslexias. Brain and Language, 27(2), 360-379.

learning_science.why: Alternating between naming sets incurs a measurable switch cost that indexes set-shifting efficiency.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Compute the alternating-minus-baseline inter-item time as a switch cost (M-SWITCHCOST) rather than crediting raw naming speed.
learning_science.source: Monsell, S. (2003). Task switching. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 7(3), 134-140.

learning_science.why: Inter-item pauses, not peak articulation, carry much of the naming-ability signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log inter-item interval variability and long hesitations as lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) rather than crediting the single fastest item.
learning_science.source: Kail, R., & Hall, L. K. (1994). Processing speed, naming speed, and reading. Developmental Psychology, 30(6), 949-954.

tail_precision_rationale: Naming and switch speed predict reading fluency more than g, so tail value is narrow: rhythm consistency (M-RTVAR), hesitation lapses (M-LAPSE), and the alternating switch cost (M-SWITCHCOST) index automaticity and flexible retrieval, with drift (M-DRIFT) gating engagement. It is best read as collateral fluency and set-shifting evidence and a disfluency screen, not a gifted-tail separator.
age_rationale: Holding two naming sets and switching between them under speed is unreliable at K-1, so it starts at 2-3 (alternating two colors and two objects) and extends to 6-8 (dense alphanumeric alternation). K-1 naming speed is captured by the single-category serial naming type instead; content, not motor demand, sets the band.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 alternate two colors and two objects -> 4-5 alternate letters and digits -> 6-8 dense alphanumeric alternation with confusable items
adaptive.difficulty_levers: category pair, alternation regularity (fixed ABAB vs random), grid density, item confusability, row length
adaptive.notes: Grids are generated from two item pools with a controlled alternation schedule; tap-to-advance yields rhythm, switch-cost and hesitation metrics without requiring voice capture, though optional on-device speech can corroborate.

engagement_hook: A rhythm run where the beat flips category every step - keep the groove across colors and shapes, and switch stumbles show live on a rhythm meter.
construct_irrelevant_risks: True RAN requires voice capture; tap-to-advance is a serial-scanning proxy that could be gamed by tapping without naming (mitigated by rhythm-consistency checks and optional on-device speech); item familiarity/reading level (colors and objects for pre-readers); a motor tapping-speed floor; switch cost partly reflects general set-shifting rather than pure speed.

name: Trail Namer
topics_techniques_covered: rapid_automatized_naming: follow a winding trail of repeated familiar items (colors/objects for pre-readers, letters/digits for readers) naming each stepping-stone aloud left-to-right along the path as fast as possible
rapid_automatized_naming: name a serial layout of repeated familiar objects (ball, dog, star) as fast as possible; score is total time and errors
rapid_automatized_naming: serial (path/grid) rapid naming that requires sustained scanning and eye-movements, contrasted with discrete single-item naming
one_liner: The child follows a winding trail of repeated items, tapping each stepping-stone as they name it aloud, keeping a smooth fast rhythm to the end.
interaction: A curved trail of stepping-stones (repeated colors/objects for pre-readers; letters/digits for readers) renders. The child names each stone aloud and taps it to light it and advance along the path; the current stone pulses. Each tap timestamps the inter-item interval; total time, rhythm, and hesitations are logged. Tapping is the scored channel (optional on-device speech can corroborate). Strictly ordered along the path, no skipping.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop taps along the first few stones in a steady beat with a little speech puff over each, following the winding path. One unscored warm-up segment precedes the scored trail.

learning_science.why: Serial naming speed of familiar items is a robust correlate of reading fluency and processing speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a serial trail of repeated colors/objects/letters/digits and score total time plus inter-item rhythm rather than any single fast item.
learning_science.source: Norton, E. S., & Wolf, M. (2012). Rapid automatized naming (RAN) and reading fluency. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 427-452.

learning_science.why: Serial (path/grid) naming captures the sustained scanning and eye-movement demands that discrete single-item naming misses.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A winding path enforces continuous left-to-right serial scanning with tap-to-advance, capturing the serial rhythm and hesitations.
learning_science.source: Denckla, M. B., & Rudel, R. G. (1976). Rapid automatized naming (R.A.N.): Dyslexia differentiated from other learning disabilities. Neuropsychologia, 14(4), 471-479.

learning_science.why: Inter-item pauses, not peak articulation speed, carry much of the naming-ability signal, and consistency tracks ability better than peak speed (worst-performance rule).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log inter-item-interval variability and long hesitations as lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) rather than crediting the single fastest stone.
learning_science.source: Kail, R., & Hall, L. K. (1994). Processing speed, naming speed, and reading. Developmental Psychology, 30(6), 949-954.

tail_precision_rationale: Naming speed predicts fluency more than g, so tail value is narrow and honest: rhythm consistency (M-RTVAR) and hesitation/lapse frequency (M-LAPSE) across the serial trail, plus drift (M-DRIFT), index automaticity and sustained engagement. Raw naming speed is never the score; the type is read as collateral fluency/effort evidence and a disfluency screen, and the path log (M-PATH) confirms orderly serial scanning versus erratic jumps.
age_rationale: Tap-to-advance serial naming along a path needs only sequential taps, so it spans K-1 (5-8 repeated colors or objects, pre-literacy naming) to 6-8 (letters/digits, longer denser trails). Content, not motor demand, sets the band: pre-readers name colors/objects while readers name letters/digits; the guided path lowers the visual-scan burden for the youngest.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 short trail of 5-8 repeated colors or objects -> 2-3 letters/digits on a longer trail -> 4-5 denser mixed alphanumeric -> 6-8 long dense letter/digit trails
adaptive.difficulty_levers: item type (color/object vs letter/digit), trail length, item confusability, path curvature/density
adaptive.notes: Trails are generated from an item pool along a procedural path; tap-to-advance yields rhythm and hesitation metrics without requiring voice capture, though optional on-device speech can corroborate.

engagement_hook: A hop-along-the-trail rhythm run: name and tap each stepping-stone to keep a smooth beat to the finish; hesitations break the groove and a live rhythm meter shows it.
construct_irrelevant_risks: True RAN requires voice capture; tap-to-advance is a serial-scanning proxy that could be gamed by tapping without naming (mitigated by rhythm-consistency checks and optional on-device speech); item familiarity/reading level (colors/objects for pre-readers); a motor tapping-speed floor; the guided path reduces but does not remove visual-scan variance (reported via M-PATH).

name: Card Namer
topics_techniques_covered: rapid_automatized_naming: discrete single-item rapid naming - one familiar item (color/object for pre-readers, letter/digit for readers) appears at a time; name it aloud and tap to reveal the next, as fast as possible
rapid_automatized_naming: name repeated familiar objects/colors as fast as possible (naming speed, pre-literacy for young children)
rapid_automatized_naming: contrast discrete single-item naming (isolating retrieval/articulation) against serial full-grid naming (which adds scanning and eye-movements)
one_liner: One familiar item flashes at a time; the child names it aloud and taps to flip to the next, naming a whole deck as fast as they can.
interaction: A single card shows one repeated-set item (color/object for pre-readers; letter/digit for readers). The child names it aloud and taps NEXT (or taps the card) to reveal the following card; each tap timestamps the per-card naming interval. A fixed deck length is named as fast as possible. Tapping is the scored channel; optional on-device speech can corroborate. Discrete presentation isolates retrieval/articulation from serial scanning.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a card, a little speech puff over it, then the hand tapping NEXT to flip to the following card, repeating in a steady beat. One unscored warm-up card precedes the scored deck.

learning_science.why: Naming speed of familiar items is a robust correlate of reading fluency and processing speed even in a discrete (single-item) format.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present one repeated-set item at a time and score per-card naming time plus its consistency, not any single fast card.
learning_science.source: Norton, E. S., & Wolf, M. (2012). Rapid automatized naming (RAN) and reading fluency. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 427-452.

learning_science.why: Discrete single-item naming isolates lexical retrieval and articulation, while serial naming adds scanning; contrasting them separates the retrieval component from the scanning component.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a one-card-at-a-time flip so per-item retrieval time is measured cleanly, complementing the serial Trail and Grid naming types.
learning_science.source: Georgiou, G. K., Parrila, R., & Kirby, J. R. (2009). RAN components and reading development. Scientific Studies of Reading, 13(6), 508-534.

learning_science.why: Intra-individual variability and slow lapses predict ability better than the single fastest naming.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Emphasize per-card interval variability and slow-tail lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE); never score peak naming speed.
learning_science.source: Coyle, T. R. (2003). A review of the worst performance rule. Intelligence, 31(6), 567-587.

tail_precision_rationale: Naming speed predicts fluency more than g, so its tail value is narrow and honestly framed: per-card interval consistency (M-RTVAR) and slow-tail lapses (M-LAPSE), plus drift (M-DRIFT), index retrieval automaticity and sustained engagement. Discrete presentation yields a cleaner per-item retrieval time than serial naming, but raw speed is never the score; it is collateral fluency/effort evidence and, contrasted with the serial Trail/Grid types, helps separate a scanning bottleneck from a retrieval bottleneck.
age_rationale: Naming one card and tapping to advance needs only a single tap per item, so it spans K-1 (colors/objects, pre-literacy naming) to 6-8 (letters/digits, longer decks). Content, not motor demand, sets the band; discrete presentation removes the scanning load, making it the most accessible naming shell for the youngest.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 deck of repeated colors or objects -> 2-3 letters/digits -> 4-5 mixed alphanumeric -> 6-8 longer decks with confusable items
adaptive.difficulty_levers: item type (color/object vs letter/digit), deck length, item confusability, pacing/deadline
adaptive.notes: Decks are generated from an item pool; tap-to-advance yields per-card naming intervals without voice capture, though optional on-device speech can corroborate; the discrete format contrasts with the serial naming types.

engagement_hook: A flip-the-deck speed round: name each card and flick to the next, racing a per-card rhythm meter; steady clean naming beats frantic stumbling.
construct_irrelevant_risks: True RAN requires voice capture; tap-to-advance is a proxy that could be gamed by flipping without naming (mitigated by rhythm-consistency checks and optional on-device speech); item familiarity/reading level (colors/objects for pre-readers); a motor tapping-speed floor; the discrete format removes serial-scan variance by design, which also means it under-samples the scanning component captured by the Trail/Grid types.

name: Blink Hunt
topics_techniques_covered: symbol_search: a target symbol is shown, then a small array flashes briefly and is masked; report whether the target was present among the distractors (present/absent visual search)
symbol_search: scan a search group for whether a target symbol is present, with set size and target-distractor similarity as difficulty levers
inspection_time: the array is shown for a staircased brief exposure then backward-masked, so the manipulated variable is perceptual intake time, not motor speed
symbol_search: visual search where accuracy scales with set size and target-distractor similarity
one_liner: A target symbol is shown, then a little group of symbols flashes for a split second and is hidden by a mask; the child calmly says whether the target was in the group.
interaction: A target symbol pins at the top. An array of symbols then flashes for a staircased exposure and is overwritten by a pattern mask. Only after the mask does the child tap a large YES (target was present) or NO (absent); the response itself is untimed (motor-free). Exposure shortens as the child succeeds. Tapping only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the pinned target, an array flashing then a mask dropping, and the hand calmly tapping YES (the target had been there) with a checkmark - emphasizing the answer is unhurried. One unscored warm-up with a long exposure precedes the staircase.

learning_science.why: Detecting a target among distractors depends on set size and target-distractor similarity, giving a graded, calibratable perceptual-search difficulty.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale set size and distractor similarity, and key each trial as target-present or target-absent for a sensitivity measure.
learning_science.source: Treisman, A., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

learning_science.why: Placing the search behind a staircased brief exposure and a backward mask makes the manipulated variable perceptual intake time, largely removing motor/response speed from the score.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Backward-mask the array after a staircased exposure and let the child answer at leisure; estimate the exposure threshold (M-ITTHRESH).
learning_science.source: Deary, I. J., & Stough, C. (1996). Intelligence and inspection time. American Psychologist, 51(6), 599-608.

learning_science.why: Present/absent judgements conflate sensitivity with a yes/no response bias, which must be separated so a cautious child and a guesser are not scored alike.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Compute d-prime from hits and false alarms across target-present and target-absent trials (M-DPRIME, M-FALSEALARM).
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: This blends the least motor-confounded speed signal (inspection-time threshold, M-ITTHRESH; a modest but clean link to g) with search sensitivity: d-prime (M-DPRIME) and false-alarm control (M-FALSEALARM) separate true masked detection from guessing and from a yes/no bias, and matched parallel trials (M-CONSIST) tighten the estimate at the cut. Because the response is untimed and motor-free, the score reflects perceptual intake and search sensitivity, never impulsive fast tapping; it is offered as a corroborating perceptual-speed adjunct, not a standalone tail decider.
age_rationale: The masked present/absent response is untimed and motor-free, so difficulty is perceptual, not motor. It fits 2-3 (a large distinct target among 1-2 dissimilar distractors, long ~300-400 ms exposures) to 6-8 (confusable distractors, larger sets, short staircased exposures). K-1 is excluded because reliably understanding the flash-then-mask rule and holding a target in mind is unreliable that young; K-1 speed is captured by the matching, sweep, whack, and naming types.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 one distinct target among 1-2 dissimilar distractors, ~300-400 ms -> 4-5 moderate similarity and set size, ~150-250 ms -> 6-8 confusable distractors, larger sets, staircased toward ~30-80 ms
adaptive.difficulty_levers: pre-mask exposure duration (staircase), set size, target-distractor similarity, mask strength, proportion of target-present trials
adaptive.notes: Symbols are drawn from a large glyph pool with a tunable similarity metric and a balanced present/absent key; a 2-down/1-up staircase converges on the ~71% threshold, so items are infinitely cloneable and the threshold plus d-prime are robust statistics.

engagement_hook: A blink-and-catch spy game: the lineup flashes for a heartbeat then vanishes behind static - was your target in there? The flash gets shorter every round.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Display refresh rate limits the shortest true exposure (report the threshold with the measured frame time); ambient brightness and visual acuity; a yes/no response bias (mitigated by a balanced present/absent key and d-prime reporting); sustained-attention lapses (engagement gated via M-ENGAGE); it is among the least motor-confounded speed tasks because the response is untimed.

name: Blink Spotter
topics_techniques_covered: symbol_search: a target symbol is shown, then an array flashes briefly and is masked; tap WHERE the target had appeared (localize the target among distractors)
symbol_search: visual search for a target among distractors where accuracy scales with set size and target-distractor similarity
inspection_time: the array is shown for a staircased brief exposure then backward-masked, so the manipulated variable is perceptual intake time rather than motor/response speed
symbol_search: find the target among distractors, moving from a distinct target to confusable foils as difficulty rises
one_liner: A target is shown, then a grid of symbols flashes for a split second and is hidden; the child calmly taps the spot where the target had been.
interaction: A target symbol pins at the top. A small grid of symbols (one is the target) flashes for a staircased exposure and is overwritten by a pattern mask, leaving empty outlined cells. Only after the mask does the child tap the CELL where the target had appeared; the response is untimed (motor-free). Exposure shortens as the child succeeds. Tapping only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the pinned target, a grid flashing then masking to empty cells, and the hand calmly tapping the cell where the target had been (a checkmark confirms) - emphasizing the answer is unhurried. One unscored warm-up with a long exposure precedes the staircase.

learning_science.why: Locating a target among distractors depends on set size and target-distractor similarity, giving a graded, calibratable perceptual-search difficulty.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale grid size and distractor similarity; the localization response yields a chance baseline that scales with set size.
learning_science.source: Treisman, A., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

learning_science.why: Putting the search behind a staircased brief exposure and a backward mask makes perceptual intake time the manipulated variable, largely removing motor/response speed from the score.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Backward-mask the grid after a staircased exposure and let the child answer at leisure; estimate the exposure threshold (M-ITTHRESH).
learning_science.source: Vickers, D., Nettelbeck, T., & Willson, R. J. (1972). Perceptual indices of performance. Perception, 1(3), 263-295.

learning_science.why: The flash-then-locate rule must be obvious without any text so novelty variance is not measured.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A wordless ghost-hand demo shows the flash, the mask, and a calm tap on the remembered location before scoring.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59-89.

tail_precision_rationale: Localization under masking blends the least motor-confounded speed signal (inspection-time threshold, M-ITTHRESH) with spatial visual search: because the response is untimed and motor-free, accuracy at short exposures reflects perceptual intake and search efficiency, not tapping speed. Error type (M-ERRTYPE: an adjacent-cell miss - correct region, imprecise - versus a random-cell miss) flags near-misses that mark latent ability just under the cut, and matched parallel trials (M-CONSIST) tighten the threshold at the cut. It is a corroborating perceptual-speed adjunct, never a standalone decider.
age_rationale: The masked localization response is untimed and motor-free, so difficulty is perceptual, not motor. It fits 2-3 (a distinct target in a 2x2 grid, long ~300-400 ms exposures) to 6-8 (confusable distractors in larger grids, short staircased exposures). K-1 is excluded because the flash-then-locate rule is unreliable that young; K-1 speed is captured by the matching, sweep, whack, and naming types.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 distinct target in a 2x2 grid, ~300-400 ms -> 4-5 moderate similarity in a 3x3, ~150-250 ms -> 6-8 confusable distractors in a larger grid, staircased toward ~30-80 ms
adaptive.difficulty_levers: pre-mask exposure duration (staircase), grid size, target-distractor similarity, mask strength
adaptive.notes: Grids are generated from a glyph pool with a tunable similarity metric and a known target cell; a 2-down/1-up staircase converges on the ~71% threshold, so items are infinitely cloneable and the threshold is a robust statistic; chance level is 1/cells.

engagement_hook: A blink-and-point memory-flash game: the grid lights up for a heartbeat then hides - can you still point to where your target was? The flash keeps getting shorter.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Display refresh rate limits the shortest true exposure (report the threshold with the measured frame time); ambient brightness and visual acuity; motor mis-tap on small cells (large cells, generous hit-boxes, adjacent-miss logged separately via M-ERRTYPE); sustained-attention lapses (engagement gated via M-ENGAGE); it is among the least motor-confounded speed tasks because the response is untimed.

name: Light Racer
topics_techniques_covered: simple_reaction_time: at the start line one lane light turns green after a jittered ready-hold and the child slaps GO the instant it lights, over many trials, recording mean and (critically) the variability of response time
choice_reaction_time: one of two then four lane lights turns green and the child taps the lane that lit, a fast low-reading choice reaction whose response time rises with the number of lanes

choice_reaction_time: reaction across 1, 2 and 4 lanes so the slope of response time against log2(number of lanes) indexes information-processing rate (Hick's law) while the intercept absorbs motor/device latency

simple_reaction_time: derive intra-individual RT variability (SD and slow-tail lapses) from the speeded start block; per the worst-performance rule a child's slowest starts, not their fastest, carry the ability signal
one_liner: At a racing start line the child waits, coiled, then slaps the lane the instant its light flicks green - jumping early is a false start.
interaction: One (simple) or several (choice) lane lights sit at the start line. After a jittered ready-hold one light flicks green; the child taps the large GO pad (single lane) or the lane that lit (two or four lanes). A tap before the light is a false start (flagged and excluded from RT); too slow is a miss. Brief feedback, then the next start. Tapping only, on large fixed pads.
